questions.question: What is the DOM and how do you update it safely?
questions.title: DOM tree and safe updates
questions.direct_answer: The DOM is the browser's in-memory object model of a document. Safe updates target the smallest relevant node, use textContent for plain untrusted text, create elements with DOM APIs, and avoid repeatedly replacing a large subtree.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the DOM model, targeted updates, and safe text insertion.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Sending untrusted text through innerHTML or rebuilding a parent whose children hold state and listeners.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: DOM updates run on the browser's main thread; large synchronous batches can delay input and rendering.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The DOM represents the document as connected node objects.
Select the smallest stable element that owns the change.
Use textContent for plain text and createElement for new structure.
Group related writes and avoid replacing an entire subtree for one small update.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The DOM is the browser's object model for a document. HTML elements, text, and other document parts become connected node objects that JavaScript can read, create, move, or remove.

A safe update changes the smallest piece that owns the new state. Plain user-provided text belongs in `textContent`, while new structure can be created with `createElement`, configured through properties, and inserted with `append` or `replaceChildren`.

For example, a status component can keep its existing element, set its text to “Saved,” and add a success class. That preserves unrelated siblings and avoids parsing the message as markup.

Replacing a large parent with `innerHTML` can destroy descendant object identity, form state, and listeners attached directly to those descendants. Many DOM operations also occupy the main thread, so large updates should be measured and split or batched when needed.

The practical rule is targeted, typed DOM operations for normal UI changes, with HTML parsing reserved for content that has a deliberate trust and sanitization boundary.

sections.title: The DOM is a mutable tree
sections.content: Each node knows where it sits in the document and can expose parent, child, and sibling relationships. Changing a property changes the model; the browser then decides which style, layout, paint, or compositing work is necessary. A JavaScript write does not always force every rendering stage.

sections.title: Safe DOM content and structure boundaries
sections.content: Text is data, so `textContent` inserts it literally. Structure is a set of nodes, so `createElement` and `append` make that intent visible. Parsing an HTML string combines both and creates an injection boundary. For a long list, build the nodes away from the live parent and attach them together, but measure before assuming a fragment is faster than modern browser optimizations.

sections.title: A safe update path
sections.content:
New value
  ├─ plain text → `textContent`
  ├─ known structure → `createElement` + properties + `append`
  └─ trusted or sanitized HTML → reviewed parsing boundary
                 ↓
       browser recalculates affected rendering work

questions.question: When should you use textContent instead of innerHTML?
questions.title: textContent versus innerHTML
questions.direct_answer: Use textContent when the value should be plain text, especially when it comes from a user, API, URL, or database. innerHTML parses a string as markup and replaces an element's descendants, so it belongs only at a deliberate trusted or sanitized HTML boundary.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to choose a DOM insertion API according to content type and trust.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Escaping only script tags before assigning untrusted input to innerHTML.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: textContent cannot create formatting; genuinely rich content needs safe node construction or a reviewed sanitization and Trusted Types strategy.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: textContent inserts a value as literal text.
innerHTML parses markup and replaces all descendant nodes.
Untrusted strings must not be assigned directly to innerHTML.
Use DOM construction or a trusted sanitization boundary for rich content.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `textContent` and `innerHTML` answer different questions. `textContent` treats a value as text, while `innerHTML` treats it as HTML source, parses it, and replaces the element's descendants with the parsed nodes. Plain labels, names, messages, and API values should normally use `textContent`. For example, the string `` appears literally when assigned to textContent, but it becomes an element with an event handler when carelessly parsed as HTML. `innerHTML` is also a structural replacement. Existing descendant nodes are removed, so references, input state, and event listeners attached directly to those old nodes may no longer describe what is on screen. Rich HTML is a valid requirement, but its trust boundary must be explicit. Known markup can be built with DOM methods; untrusted markup needs a maintained sanitizer and, where supported, an enforced Trusted Types policy or a safe sanitizing API. The choice is simple: use textContent for text, node APIs for known structure, and HTML parsing only when both the source and security controls are understood.

sections.title: Parsing is the meaningful difference
sections.content: The visual output of the two properties can look identical for a simple word, which hides their different semantics. The difference appears as soon as the string contains markup characters, descendant elements, or an attack payload. Treating the value by its intended type avoids relying on fragile filtering.

sections.title: Why replacing descendants has side effects
sections.content: Setting innerHTML asks the HTML parser to create an entirely new descendant tree. A button that looked unchanged can now be a different node object, so a listener registered on the old button is gone. Event delegation on a stable ancestor survives that replacement because the ancestor listener remains. Node construction can preserve identity by updating or replacing only the pieces that actually changed.

sections.title: Choose by content type
sections.content:
| Need | Safer API | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Plain text | `textContent` | No HTML parsing |
| Known element structure | `createElement` + `append` | Explicit nodes and properties |
| Reviewed rich HTML | Sanitizing API or TrustedHTML policy | Parsed after a trust check |
| Read current markup | `innerHTML` getter | Serialized descendants, not listeners |
